utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is the case number IT-98-29-T, the Prosecutor versus Stanislav Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we ended last Friday during the cross-examination of the witness, Mr. Ashton. Would you be prepared to proceed? I see that Ms. Pilipovic is standing. Is there anything you would like to --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we're not receiving the B/C/S interpretation on the sixth channel, so I wasn't able to hear you just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The problem with the B/C/S interpretation is caused by any technical problem or the absence of interpreters? I can't see through the dark windows.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters are present.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Thank you very much. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I'll ask the usher to call in the witness and you may proceed in the cross-examination of Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, before we bring in the witness, I should like to make two remarks concerning the problem of interpretation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Go ahead, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President. The first of my remarks will be presented with my apologies, because you were able to see in the transcript, in the English transcript yesterday -- I'm not giving you the references because it's not that important, but you were able to see that I was rephrasing a question, or rather, asking the question once again concerning the missiles, but I was actually referring to mortar shells, and the logical interpretation should have been a shell instead of "missile." Every time I will be referring to the shelling of Sarajevo, I won't be using the word "missile." That is one of the remarks that I wanted to make. The other one being something that you, Your Honour, has mentioned. It is something that I paid attention to over the weekend. There seems to have been a problem in the interpretation. I was not referring to the day after but to something else. I will -- I hope that we will be able to clarify the issue today during the cross-examination of the witness. I don't have any other remarks to make, and otherwise I'm ready to proceed with my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Usher, would you please bring in Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I remind you that you are still bound by the solemn declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me continue where we left off last time by asking you the following question: Is it true that you were interviewed on the 29th, 30th, and 31st of October, 2001, also on the 1st of November, 2001, then the 12th, the 13th, and the 14th of November, 2001, concerning previous incidents that you were able to experience in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those are the dates of the interview, yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. Is it true that you signed each of the pages -- each page of your written statement?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I signed the pages of my statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When you were introduced to the person who -- I'm sorry. When you were presenting the facts about these incidents to the person who interviewed you, did you present those facts in a chronological order, generally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. So in principle, we can conclude that the incidents were presented according to a chronological order?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because there were some incidents that I recall that fell into place outside the chronological order.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like the written statement of the witness to be shown to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We can actually present to him the whole statement or parts of it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that at the beginning we can show him just one portion of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The short part, you had better read it; if it's a longer part, then of course you'll have to tender that into evidence later on if you present it to the witness or at least have it marked for identification. I don't know what your intention is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it will be about five pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Five pages. You had better present it to the witness. Is the Prosecution aware of the statement that will be provided to the witness, date --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The origin of the statement is the Office of the Prosecutor and I just mentioned the relevant dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The statements of all these dates?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I'm really sorry, but I'm listening at the same time to the English interpretation. Would you please follow the transcript so that I can answer to your question? I'm sorry. I did not hear your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you were presenting statements of several dates or of a specific date?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The first pages, Mr. President, are grouped under three dates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which will take me only 30 seconds to locate the pages in question. To be more precise, I am referring to the 12th, the 13th, and the 14th of November, 2001. I should like to show these few pages to the witness at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you like to have them marked for identification or are you going to present them --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will see, Your Honour, at the end of the testimony. Internal numbers for the Prosecution are as follows: 0212, 9568.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have any copies for the Bench, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me find my copies, Mr. President. I should like to state that we've had a technical problem; however, everything is here. I hope that everyone has got their copies. Is there a problem with the interpretation? Very well. May I continue, though I can see that my colleague is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, at line 11, said that he was referring to the statement of the 12th, 13th, and the 14th of November, 2001. That is correct in that the pages which he has identified were attached to the statement signed on the 14th of November, but more particularly, those pages come from the statement signed on the 1st of November, 2001 by the witness, which was attached to the later statement. So I rise to my feet to clarify that the pages which my friend has provided to the witness in fact come from the statement signed on the 1st of November, 2001. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't think the main issue is at what time and what date exactly they were signed but that we are not mistaken as far as the pages are concerned. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you please indicate always by the last four figures the page you're referring to. So if you're asking anything about 9568, then please indicate that it was 9568 or 9569 or -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll be happy to do that, Mr. President. However, let me indicate that we've had a problem with the photocopying machine here in the building, and I no longer have the relevant numbers in front of me. But I will be referring to the document that you yourself have in front of you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, on the pages that you have in front of you, do you recognise your signature?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognise my signature.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is it true that one can follow the incidents that were the subject of the statement in a chronological order, formally speaking?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe the -- all the incidents are in chronological order in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question, please. Is it not true that in this document you were talking about an incident at the beginning which took place at the beginning of July, then as we progress in the statement, you finally speak about the moment when -- that is, the incident when you were injured?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. I believe that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So it is a chronological order, more or less?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: More or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, would you please tell us, in these two documents, what would be the incident which you referred to on Friday concerning the photograph of the attack, the photograph which was taken from the PTT building. If you don't remember the exact place, let me remind you that the last four digits are 1328?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two documents I've got, one document here -- what's the other document you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You're talking about the photograph? Would you like to see it again?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The other copy you have, if available.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, do I have to show the witness the photograph once again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of the Registry at this moment, so I'd like to ask the usher to bring the photo to the witness. This is approximately in the middle of the bundle, Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay. I have the photograph 1328; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: If that's a question, yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where in the document are you pointing out Friday that was reported to?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I think that I asked a question [In English] witness statement [Interpretation] And the question is as follows: In the witness statement that you have in front of you, where is the incident which concerns the photograph in question, 1328, that you also have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall in all honesty referring to this incident here in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Take your time. If you need to, you may read the text in its entirety. We are talking about the month of July, 1992?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: This photograph was not taken in July. This photograph was taken in September.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that this photograph was taken in September?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the beginning of September. Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Let me immediately follow up with another question. You stated before this Court that in Germany, in a US air force base, you had met someone that in French I would be referring to as a military liaison. When was that? On what date?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In September he was working at Sarajevo airport. He wasn't in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry. That's not my question. You stated, under oath, before this Tribunal, that you had met this person in an American base in Germany. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: When exactly was that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Early October I went -- the end of September to Germany, I went again in October to Germany. It was be sometime after that, because I had the photographs when I came back.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You also testified before this Court, sir - I do not wish to be mistaken - that it was during your stay in this American base, which took place immediately after your wounding, that is, some ten days later, the 2nd of August, 1992, to be more precise. You never testified before this Court that you had been in this American base on several occasions. Why?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because when I was working for the United Nations I had the ability to fly on any UNPROFOR flight to any one of the countries it was going to, Italy, Rhein-Main air force base, Zagreb, Split, and I made flights to Rhein-Main, I made flights to Zagreb, I made flights to Split. They're all recorded in the register at Luvkomet [phoen] is he Sarajevo airport. Every time one of us got on the flights we would have to sign in, and I travelled to Germany at least five times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And on each occasion it was order to meet with officers -- strike that. On each occasion it was in order to meet with individuals on the American base in Germany?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, the witness just has stated that, for example, he went to Italy, so a question asking whether he was always seen on a German -- on German territory, other people --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll rephrase the question. I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have testified that you had seen this individual on several occasions in Germany.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. Three, to be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have also told us that the individual in question did not have permission to leave the American base; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I therefore conclude that you met with him on several occasions at this particular American base?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: For some reason, he was always at the plane when it arrived to find out who was getting on or off the plane. I assume - I don't know - he was there at the logistics end of it. I never asked that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Does that mean that you met with him on several occasions at this American base?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met with him three times, each of the three times I saw him. The first time I went out with him for drinks because I had to stay at the hotel that night on the base. That was the night we had our detailed conversation. That's the night he saw the pictures. The second time we spoke briefly. He invited me to go with him to the base bar. I didn't have time. The third time was also a brief greetings, a short conversation about his interest in going to the United States, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I ask you to tell us what you were doing at that American base? It's not because you were wounded once again, was it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Whenever any one of us, any United Nations official, and even journalists had the right to fly out on these flights to any base they wanted to go, the British, the French, the Norwegians, the Italians, the Spanish, and I flew on several other UNPROFOR flights. I flew with the French quite frequently I flew with the British to Ancona, the French to Ancona. I flew with the French to Split. I flew with the Americans from Sarajevo to Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I don't think I heard you say yesterday that on several occasions you had been to that American air force base. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not asked any question about how many times I went.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well, then. I thought I heard you say that you gave as the date of that photograph as being July.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I did not give that date as being July. This photograph was taken early September and in October I showed this to the gentleman in Rhein-Main air force base, along with some other photographs from the hospitals. I had finally put an album together the beginning of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will check that out later on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, to go back to that liaison person that we mentioned and that we now discover that you met him on several occasions, in Germany, now, was that person wearing civilian clothes or military clothes, military uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was wearing civilian clothes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why did you then say, and I quote from memory, but I will be able to look it up in the text if you contradict me, that he was wearing a uniform all the time?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said this guy wore a uniform. He never did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, with the Court's indulgence, there seem to be a number of important contradictions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... find the exact text and then you may perhaps at a later moment come back to this.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really do apologise, but as the witness has contradicted me, I must -- need to find the exact text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... perhaps you could try to find this during one of the breaks, and so that we can continue now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll find it straight away, but yes, I will go on to ask the witness another question straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I asked you -- on Friday I asked you a question, to find out whether you were treated in a hospital or private clinic in Germany. Do you remember me asking you that? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember you insinuating that I was treated in a private clinic and asking about a hospital, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it true that you answered that you had never said that you were ever treated in a private hospital? Did you say that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't say that. I said private clinic. I was not treated in a private clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What is the difference between a clinic, a private clinic, and a private hospital? Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The difference is between the question you asked on Friday. I was treated Krankenhaus Bogenhausen in Germany, in Munich Germany. That was the hospital I was treated at.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So it wasn't a private hospital?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's a State Hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And it is not a private clinic either?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, this is not the first time this witness has contradicted himself. The witness asserted, and I'm going to read it out to you in a moment, that he was treated in a private hospital, and I'll find the exact reference in just a moment. As far as the question -- as far as one of the number of contradictions are concerned, the reference is the following: The 11th of January is the date. It is a Friday, Friday the 11th of January, and the exact line in my provisional transcript is as follows, and it comes from the mouth of Mr. Ashton and it is 14:42:12, and I quote: [In English] "Therefore, I have no idea if he was or was not except for the fact that he was constantly in military clothes, every time I saw him."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me ask the question once again of you, Witness. What you said, is it correct or am I wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is not my recollection that the witness said that. We have gone on our LiveNote to the page and line provided by my friend, and I don't see the text there. I assume that this is explained by an anomaly with the software. My friend is now putting to the witness the proposition that -- more or less he's inviting the witness to agree that that's what was said. I would be grateful for an opportunity to find that passage, given -- the passage in the transcript given that's not my recollection that's what the witness said. Perhaps my friend could assist me in finding that passage by referring from his transcript as to the question which preceded that answer. That might assist us. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, may I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. On the other hand, I would allow Mr. Ierace to at least check on the source you're using at this moment. But if you can help him, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly. The document that I have before me is the transcript of Friday, the 11th of January, 2002. The question was asked at 14 hours, 41:27. And I'm going to reread the answer. But, Mr. President, the question was asked in English, the witness answered in English, and I am going to read out the quote.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've found it, Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the transcript on the LiveNote for Friday indicates the time of commencement of cross-examination, which is about 10 minutes before that time reference for my friend, so that has assisted us to try and find the passage. We're just checking for it now. If you would allow me a moment, Mr. President, I'll indicate when we've found it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As we're here, we can quote the line where the witness asserted that he was indeed treated in a private hospital, and he has just contradicted himself in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I've found a passage which confirms my recollection. On my copy of the transcript, it is page 14 -- excuse me. At least, the numbers in the margin are 1447:1. I'm unsure as to whether 14:47 refers to the time or the page number. Excuse me. I think it's the page number. And I'll read the question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not quite sure whether it is up to Mr. Ierace to read the questions and the answers out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... of importance at this moment that there's no misunderstanding about the lines you are quoting. So I'll allow Mr. Ierace to read what is in his understanding the line you're referring to, so that there will be no misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: This passage appears in the answer: "First of all, he was never a Bosnian Serb officer or a military personnel, at least he never --"

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. That's quite a different passage. I really do apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'd like to have -- could you please provide the Bench, both of you, with the pages - I don't know whether they can be printed or not - you're referring to. I want to make clear that there's no misunderstanding about what is intended by Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Since we have no provisional transcript, the Bench has no provisional transcript yet, I'd like you to present, as far as possible, the text you're referring to so that I can check whether it is the same or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can I hand the usher the document in question and the contradiction is mentioned here, as I said, at 14:41:12. That's where the contradiction appears.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, whether this is a contradiction or not will later be decided by the Bench, if necessary, and you cannot just suggest a contradiction may be there but not the contradiction as such. Could you please provide first the Prosecution with the page you're referring to, and if there's any misunderstanding, provide then the Bench with the information.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Willingly, Mr. President, and I should just like to note that we have the same documents but the Defence will be happy to help out the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm grateful for that opportunity and I'm grateful to my friend from providing the transcript, and I invite Your Honours to read it. There are two relevant pages that -- that are two relevant passages on the page which my friend has handed to me. The first is at line -- and these are the numbers on this page - 14:39:02, and in particular, 14:39:13, where these words appear: "He always wore civilian clothes." And then further down the page, at 14:42:19, these words appear: "He was constantly in military clothes, every time I saw him."

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's just what I was saying, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I haven't finished. I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Oh, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is my distinct recollection that at no stage did the witness say, on Friday, that this person always wore military clothes. In other words, it's my suspicion that there is a mistake in the transcript which will need to be checked against the tape, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course, the Prosecution may later check on whether this is a mistake in the transcript or in the translation, but I think at this moment, since the provisional transcript has to be -- the bases we work upon at this moment, I will allow Mr. Piletta-Zanin to continue questioning. There's no misunderstanding at this moment about what he's referring to and whether this is a correct line or not, you'll have the opportunity to challenge that later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have no suggestions to make to the proposal of the Prosecution, but I would like to take note of the fact that we have no problems with the translation. The Prosecution has no problems of interpretation and translation. Thank you. And that as a result, if a problem has occurred, the Prosecution reacts immediately and not three days later. Having said that, and in that same vein of thinking, witness, you have said that you were never treated in a private clinic or hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Have I misunderstood you or is that indeed what you stated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was treated in a hospital in Germany. Now, I didn't know if Krankenhaus Bogenhausen was private or public, but I believe it's a public hospital. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that it was a State Hospital. I think the term you used was State Hospital; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what Krankenhaus Bogenhausen's status is --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Would you like to go back to your statement of a moment ago, what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know what I said a moment ago. I'm just not positive -- I'm under the impression that it is, but I'm I can't answer the question because I'm not positive what the status is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: A moment ago you were more assertive in the affirmative. But let me rephrase my question. If today you do not know whether it was or was not a public hospital, how, then, were you able to assert that it was not a private clinic?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only -- I can assert that it's not a private hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But that's the answer you gave me when I asked you. Why did you give me that answer, then?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it is state or private.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Why did you tell me, categorically, in answer to one of my questions, that it wasn't a private clinic? I think you said, following on from my memory, "I never stated that I was treated in a private clinic." I think that's what you said. So why did you say that, if you weren't sure?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because that is correct. I was never treated in a private clinic. I was treated in a hospital, not a clinic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. What is the difference, sir, between a hospital and a clinic? That is also one of the questions I asked you a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: My definition of a clinic in Germany is a small institution where you go for specialised treatment. A hospital is a large institution that treats a wide variety of injuries with an emergency room and a complete medical -- it's a complete medical facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Is that the reason why you said that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Said what?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The answer we're talking about now, that you were never treated in a private clinic.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the reason I said I was never treated in a private clinic. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: But you'll agree with me that you did state that you were treated in a hospital, a private one?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was treated in a hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Private?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if it's private or state. I'm not sure if Krankenhaus Bogenhausen --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to refer back to the statement, if I may, now, or rather, the evidence, because the witness's memory seems to be shorter than our own. On the 9th of January, 2002, line 16:31:39, and I would be happy to provide the Prosecution with a copy if they are unable to find that particular line, but I shall quote, 16:31:39 is the line number [In English], "so I went to Munich, to a private German hospital, where the doctors said," And so on and so on and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Mr. Ashton, did you state, on the 9th of January of this year, at around 1600 hours, 31 minutes, 39 seconds, that you were treated in a private hospital in Munich?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Now there's clarification in the question you're asking. It's very clear to me why I responded how I did on the 9th of January. In reference, you kept trying to assert that I was treated at a military hospital, and I explained that I was not treated at a military hospital. I went to a German hospital. Whether private or state, it didn't matter. I just went -- I was not treated at a military institution. That's what I was trying to point out.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I think that you understood the question very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, would you just indicate the relevance of this questioning to the Court, because one thing is for sure, that Mr. Ashton indicated, whether state or private or military or whatever, that he was treated in a hospital which was called Bogenhausen. Could you please indicate, apart from the point you made, that in the wording of the answers given by the -- yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gladly, Mr. President, for the following reason: We don't have the name of the hospital in question. The witness stated what he stated, that is to say that he was treated in a hospital, and the name that I heard given was krankenhaus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: He said several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, I'm not quite sure. We can ask him the question again, and that's what I want to learn, actually. May I go ahead with the question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: What was the exact name, sir, of the hospital in question?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krankenhaus Bogenhausen and you will find that in Friday's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have a better memory of it now?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Bogenhausen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krankenhaus Bogenhausen.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Very well. I think there was a problem in the transcript, but we have the name now, and that's what I wanted to arrive at?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What I would like to clarify, Mr. Ashton, at this moment, in order to avoid further misunderstandings, Bogenhausen sounds very much like the name of a village or a city. Was the name of the krankenhaus, of the hospital, was Bogenhausen or was the location of the hospital in a village, city, whatever, called Bogenhausen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krankenhaus Bogenhausen sir, is on the outskirts of Munich. I believe, and I'm not positive, so I can't tell you the exact, but I believe it's in the Bogenhausen district of Munich. It's an area of Munich.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are you aware of any other hospitals in Bogenhausen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, let me go back to my questions and the list thereof. We seem to have lost a great deal of time in clearing up that contradiction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When you're trying to find your next question, I would like to draw your attention to what, in my mind, may be a mistaken translation. I'd like to take you back to a line which is indicated as 9:32:14.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which date, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You ordered us to react immediately, so that's what we are doing, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. So I've got on 9:32:14, in my recollection, the witness has not stated a hospital is a large institution that treats a wide variety of injuries, but, as far as I understood, he was referring to a wide variety of types of treatment needed and not just injuries. I don't know whether this is also the recollection of the parties. If this is true, we might correct it right away.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. That's the recollection of Mr. Blaxill alongside me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I admit that I did not quite take your point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The point is that it is referring to various types of injuries, where I thought that the witness was referring to various types of illnesses in need of treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Now, what I didn't understand, Mr. President, is why you indicated that it was a problem of translation, interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In my recollection, but if it's not true, of course you can check the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's the word "translation" that rather surprised me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. I think it has not great relevance. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, you stated, and I'm referring back to your accident on the 23rd of July, 1992, that you were escorted by some seven men. Is that right? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seven directly with me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You mentioned, in English, concerning those seven people, I think you used the term "team." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the term "team." I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: May I quote once again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may always quote, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Yes, you may always quote.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you profoundly.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: We're talking about the day of the 9th of January, 9th of January, 2002, and you indicated the following: [In English] "At that point, the team I was travelling with," et cetera, et cetera. [Interpretation] Can you firm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace is on his feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'd be grateful if my friend could give pages and line references.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please do so, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am going to give you the line in due course. I think it is 16:28:10. But we have no page indication on this provisional document. But let me quote again "at that point, the team I was travelling with," et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you in fact use that term "team," sir? Yes or no, please?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall the word "team." I mean, group, team. I use the same interactively.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The word "team" or "group" meant the people in question; is that right? You were referring to them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Team or group, yes. I was with a group.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The seven people that I mentioned a moment ago?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You stated before this Tribunal that the five policemen who were accompanying you did not carry weapons. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And you've just told me that the word "team" or "group" designated the same thing, that is to say, the people who were accompanying you, and there were seven of them, and you stated, after the quotation that I just quoted a moment ago, you go on to say [In English], "Had time to get their weapons up and return fire." [Interpretation] End of quotation. I therefore take it, following on from your explanations, that the team that you were saying numbered seven persons was armed because you stated that they were able to return fire. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Haven't you told me a moment ago that the word "team" that you used concerned the group of people that accompanied you -- meant the group of people that accompanied you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You phrased this last statement, this last question, they raised their weapons and returned fire. I never indicated who raised their weapons and returned fire. I did indicate -- I don't know if in this testimony, but I did indicate that the HVO soldiers who were in front of us raised their weapons and returned fire. The police officers --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I asked a very precise question of you. I asked you about the team, and you told me that you had spoken about a group of people. We knew that there were seven of them, and you stated, I'm going to read once again, if necessary [In English], "And at that point the team that I was travelling with had time to get their weapons." [Interpretation] And you've just told me that the word "team" in English corresponded to the group of seven people who accompanied you. Is it true that you stated that the police officers in civilian clothes who accompanied you were not armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The police officers who accompanied me were not armed. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How is it possible, then, that the group was able to return fire, if they were not armed?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: One HVO officer was with the group. He was in front of me. And there were three more HVO officers -- or I shouldn't say officers. I should say soldiers, were in front of them, that were not with our group but they were moving in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have testified, Mr. Ashton, that you only had two soldiers as your escort, two soldiers in uniform. Now I'm discovering that there were more of them. It seems that we have at least five soldiers in uniform.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there were not five soldiers in uniform. There were two soldiers. One soldier escorting us, one in front of him, and then there were two HVO soldiers waiting on the opposite side of the intersection for us to cross. All in total there were four HVO soldiers and five policemen in civilian clothes, without weapons. The HVO soldiers were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you talking about the four persons who were ahead of you, who preceded you in order to cross the street?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I submit that that question does not reflect the evidence and it presumes to reflect the evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you please say in what respect it doesn't reflect the evidence? We haven't got the transcript in front of us, the transcript of Friday. Are you referring to today's --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'm referring to the answer given by this witness which appears on the LiveNote at page 26, from line 3, at 10.02 and 40 seconds. The evidence is to the effect -- I'm sorry. 10.03 and 2 seconds. That evidence is to the effect that there was one soldier escorting the witness and the civilian-dressed police officers, one in front of him, and then two on the other side of the intersection. The question put by my friend refers to the four persons who were ahead of you. In fact, the evidence is not that there were four people in front of him but one military person with them, another just in front, and then two much further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: On the other side of the intersection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There might be some misunderstanding as far as the four or two people are concerned. Could you please rephrase the question as such, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, so that everyone is happy with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I don't know whether the objection has been sustained or overruled, because as far as I remember --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I'm trying not to waste too much time. So if you were in a position to rephrase your question so that everybody could be happy with it, we don't have to give a decision, we don't have to check every single detail of the last 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me quote, and it won't be the first time today. And I quote once again, 16:26:41: [In English], "Then we moved --" let me quote another passage, line 16:27:12 [In English], "And when we got into the street, four men in front of me went across, and there were several behind me." [Interpretation] The question that I asked before I was interrupted by the Prosecution concerned those four individuals. I don't know whether Mr. Ierace maintains his objection now or not, but I think we have the same text, Mr. Ierace, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm seeking to discover that passage. Unfortunately, the transcript which is made available after the day of hearing does not have times on it, and my friend refers constantly to times. If, Mr. President, you will allow me just a moment, I think I can reasonably quickly locate that passage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will be happy to quote the relevant passage once again, if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I've found the passage. My friend now says that when he referred to four people in front, he was referring to this passage in the transcript. Now, that was not at all clear to me, and I presume to the witness, and I presume to Your Honours. It followed on references to the military people who were accompanying the witness, as well as those on the other side of the intersection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you stand by your objection, Mr. Ierace; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes. I object to the previous question that was asked. My friend has now clarified, for all our benefit, which four people he was referring to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been clarified by now. I think the objection should be denied. I'm just looking to my fellow Judges. Since there's whatever misunderstanding there might have been is not there any more. You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So before I was interrupted, Mr. Ashton, I told you that there had been four individuals in front of you, and now you are telling us that these four individuals were military men. It's a question.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four military individuals on the -- in front of me in the position -- in the angle -- in the direction I was going. There were five men in civilian clothes behind me unarmed. There were other soldiers very close by, within five, six metres away, but I did not pay attention to who they were, what they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do I understand you correctly, in fact, in front of you, you had four individuals in uniform, which made up a team, and a certain number of other people, also in uniform, behind you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said the five civilian -- men behind me were in civilian clothes, not in uniform, as you've stated in this question. I'm sorry to correct you, but this is what you've stated here. The four men in front of me were in uniform; that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you stated that you only had two military men in uniform as your escort.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have stated that the four men in front of me were a team. That's not the way I saw it. They were not a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The word "team" comes from your own testimony, but this is not a question. My question concerned four soldiers or four men in uniform in front of you. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were four men in front of me in uniform. That is correct. One was with a group I was travelling with and the other three were individuals who were going the same direction but crossed the street before I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So am I correct in concluding that this was just an occasional escort?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "occasional"?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: An escort which was not with you at all times.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Nevertheless, these soldiers were very close to you at the time of the incident?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So why didn't you therefore mention in your testimony that there was a group of at least five military men during this incident who were close to you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were only four directly related to me, and five civilian -- five men in civilian clothes that were identified to me as police officers. One was a friend, the other four were his friends, and that's all I can tell you. Now, there were other soldiers in the area, as I stated before. I don't even know how many there were. There were others I saw in uniform, very close by.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you're saying that there were four men in uniform who were close by?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In front of me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: And only one of them was a member of your escort. That is what you have just stated?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was travelling in front of us, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So other members of your escort were behind you, the second one, that is, the second person who escorted you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person behind me was my friend Sonni who was a police officer off-duty from Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: You have told us that you had two soldiers in uniform as your escorts. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was one directly in front of me in uniform that was part of the group, but there was another one that joined us before we got to the intersection, there were two at the intersection. The four of them crossed the intersection and I followed. That's when I was shot.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Five or four people with you, armed and in uniform?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five people behind me in civilian clothes. There was one in front of me who was talking to our team, our group, however you want to phrase that. He was moving with us. There was one -- we joined us, just before we got to the intersection, he joined up with us --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will ask the question for the third time, I believe now.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Four or five people in uniform with weapons that were with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was only one person in uniform with me. There were four people in uniform in front of me, going the same direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: How far from you were they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first fellow was right in front of me, who was travelling with us. He was in an HVO uniform. The second gentleman we caught up with. He was about five metres in front of us. And then the other two gentlemen were at the intersection. We caught up with them. They talked, the four gentlemen talked to each other. They warned me of the danger of crossing the intersection. And then one by one they ran across. Two of them waited on the other side before anyone else did anything. We talked a little bit there. And then the third one and the fourth one went and then I went. They were not escorts. Just the one soldier was actually an escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me remind you that you testified the other day that you had had two escorts. Is my memory correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two HVO officers or soldiers that joined links before we got to the intersection, yes. There was a second one that joined us.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me ask a different question at this point, Mr. Ashton, whether any civilians in Sarajevo, during your stay there in Sarajevo, who wore camouflage clothes, or as certain armies call it, the leopard-patterned uniform.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't recall seeing any of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Are you absolutely positive about that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To my recollection, I'm absolutely positive about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Sir, I am referring to individuals who worked for or within the army when I talk about camouflage pattern clothes?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe you said civilian. No, I did not see civilians. No. Army soldiers is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm talking about civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Let me try and understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The question is very simple. Did you ever see, at any point in time during your stay in Sarajevo, any civilian, irrespective of their gender or age, wearing camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you consider police officers civilians, they had a blue camouflage --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I'm not talking about police officers. I'm talking about civilians. I will ask the question for the third time. Did you ever see civilians, regardless of their sex or age, in Sarajevo during the time that you spent there in Sarajevo, who wore camouflage uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. My friend says -- yes. My friend says this is the third time he's asked the question. The first time he asked it, he confined it to civilians who, "Worked for or within the army." I'd be grateful if my friend could make clear whether at this stage he still confines his reference to civilians to those who were in the employment of the army. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "civilian," I'm referring to a civilian. Once again, let me ask my question. My question concerns civilians.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just try to find out, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, what this misunderstanding is about. If you're talking about civilian persons, you can think of their formal status not being military people, not being police officers. You can also understand civilians as those who are not on duty if there was any military position or any police position during duty hours. So I'd like you to clearly identify what you understand by "civilian" and not just by saying that civilians are civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, in your statement, you stated that very often civilians were targeted by isolated shots and/or shelling. Whom did you have in mind when you say "civilians"?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Civilians as defined by this question were people who were in their daily clothes to go to work, women in dresses, their coats, kids in T-shirts, pants, just no uniforms at all, just as an average person on the street here in The Hague would look walking to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you're defining a civilian only by presence of a uniform?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I object, Mr. President. I presume my friend means only by the absence of a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think that's what you had in mind, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I said by presence of a uniform, one can also interpret that if a uniform is present, we are not talking about a civilian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Mr. Ashton, I do understand that you understood by "civilians" that people who could not be identified from their appearance, especially as far as clothing was concerned, as anything other than civilians, so no military uniforms, no police uniforms; just ordinary civilian clothing, as you find it every day on the street. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm very grateful to you, Mr. President, for this clarification. At this point I should like to show the witness a document that we intend to tender as an exhibit. Yes, as an exhibit. The document will be D12. It consists of several pages. It is a written statement by Mr. Roy Thomas, which was provided for by the Prosecution. I should like the witness to read out to you, Your Honours, what was declared in the statement, if this is possible, by Mr. Roy Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is this just a few lines or is this a long --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like him to read only three lines, more or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the context of the document as such that you -- of course, you are free to tender it into evidence, but if it's just about the three lines, I don't think there's any specific need for that, unless of course the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So may I read them out directly, if you wish me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... dealing with at this moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 00552646 is the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you have a copy so that perhaps the Prosecution could just follow your reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think the original could be, for the time being, be returned to the Defence, if they're just quoting a few lines. Mr. Ierace, is it clear enough for you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, it's certainly legible, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, I am now going to read to you what was stated by another witness, Mr. Thomas Frances Roy, who was also in Sarajevo as an officer, I believe. He stated the following: [In English] "One of the problems with this was the question of who was a soldier. Many people, including women and children, wore camouflage, and then, many people who were military wore civilian clothes." [Interpretation] Have you understood this quotation, sir?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand the quotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you think that the witness didn't see things as they were or it was you who perhaps did not observe civilians wearing camouflage?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not observe civilians wearing camouflage. I don't recollect any civilian that I saw wearing camouflage, especially women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. On the other hand, you testified that some soldiers wearing a uniform --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: In line 10:27:30, you used the word "another witness, Mr. Thomas Frances Roy." He is not a witness, so as you are referring to this witness afterwards, it is better to avoid the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour. I should have used a different term. I should have said by another statement -- in another statement. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Let me now go back to what you stated, sir. In response to a question asked of you by the Prosecution, you stated that at the beginning of the hostilities, a certain number of soldiers of Bosnian forces would move from one location to another without weapons, without carrying any arms, because of a shortage of weapons. Do you abide by what you have said?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, again I object. I'd be grateful for a reference, and a reference that is useful to us, in other words, one which enables us to find the passage. I particularly rise to my feet on this occasion because, at least to me, that question doesn't make sense. A particular piece of evidence from this witness does not spring to mind in response to that question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please specify the source of your reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this an objection by Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... and I invited you to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me then try to find ... I will need some time to do that. Let me quote once again. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're quoting for the first time. You were referring to a statement. You are quoting for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but I just wanted to say that that was not the first time that I'm quoting something today. Thank you. [In English] "Most of them were not armed because at that point in the war they didn't have any weapons except the ones on the front line, which they traded." Mr. Ierace, the reference is 16:48, January 9th, 2002. The Defence will be happy to give you a hard copy if you need. What is the decision of the Court regarding the objection raised by Mr. Ierace?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You have now identified the source. I would like Mr. Ierace to confirm that he could find it or otherwise you provide him with a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, in the interests of saving time, I don't require a further reference at this stage. We have some recollection of those words now that we have been given the quote, and we are content for it to proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has the objection been rejected?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been sustained to the extent that you had to specify in more detail the source of your reference, and since you have done so, there is no objection which remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me ask the question once again, that is, for the second time.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Do you confirm this? If I understand you correctly, there were soldiers who could find themselves in town, on duty, active, but without weapons.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your answer. In respect of this same passage, you, I believe, used the word "stress," but I will check if necessary, that the army was under pressure. Is that correct? I'm referring to the army of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you read the whole statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: By all means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, this might be a suitable moment for this Chamber at this moment to have a break, and this will give you the opportunity not only to find the source of the statement -- the testimony you're referring to at this moment. But I will not allow you any more to put questions without giving clear, specified sources of the references you are making. And please make available to yourself as well hard copies for the Prosecution so that if there's any technical problem in finding immediately the source, that you can hand it over to the Prosecution. Let's not forget that I think we lost at least 10 to 15 minutes this morning just by trying to find our sources. Proper preparation of cross-examination means that if you can refer to the testimony given before while preparing it, you also can write down the exact source and have the lines literally available so that any misunderstanding will be avoided. We'll adjourn until 11.00. --- Break taken at 10.38 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, assuming that you found the source you wanted to refer to in putting the last name -- the last question to the witness, I'll give you the opportunity to proceed as soon as the witness has been brought into the courtroom. Mr. Usher is already ... Madam Registrar, the usher is --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is this an issue -- is there any objection against the witness being brought in?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was simply this: The Defence is paying great attention to citing -- quoting from the text exactly, and we are ready to provide the text, but I would just like to note that there seems to be a technical difficulty in the sense that we have transcripts with certain numbers, that is to say, date and hour numbers, and I was given to understand that the Prosecution has a different form of transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... unless you have another solution, because I'm more solution-directed than problem-directed. Will there be a possibility of having all the same provisional transcripts? Madam Registrar, do you think that this would be ... Sorry. We're just wondering, we see that two different kinds of provisional transcripts are used by the parties. Are they in the same language, Mr. Piletta-Zanin?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: The one I have is in English. I think it's the same language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So could proper attention be paid to the fact that the parties at this moment have different types of provisional transcripts, and so that they get the same, in order not to lose any more time in refining the sources.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour, I'll just call up the transcript coordinators and I asked them to bring up six copies of the transcript now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So we have copies even for the Bench so we can follow your quarrelling about the sources. Then, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if there's no other matter, then the usher may bring in Mr. Ashton.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, whilst he's being brought in, could I merely ask what time is the next break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, if I may correct you, --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Oh, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next break, I intended to have the next break after one hour and 20 minutes from 11.00, so I would say at -- let me just check.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I would say half past 12.00 or a little bit before, so that another hour remains after that short break. Yes. Thank you. Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for giving me the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] With reservations as to the exactitude and correspondence, actually, of the documents in question, with that proviso, the quotations that I'm going to make with respect to the term "stress" corresponds, looking at my lines, 17:14:31. Those are my figures. And the transcript is dated the 9th of January, 2002. So I'm going to quote the passage in question, with your permission, Your Honour. May I proceed, Your Honour? Thank you. [In English] "They were terribly stressed along the front lines, so you didn't see many of them in the city." [Interpretation] That is line 17:14:31, and the following one. I am referring to this passage of your testimony, Witness, and if I understood you correctly, you were indicating that the majority of the soldiers at that particular point in time were at the front lines or front line, rather.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but, Your Honour, there may be a mistranslation here. I may have said "stressed," but I thought I said "stretched." The interpreter may have gotten that wrong and --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It wasn't an interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It would be a matter of the transcript. If you think that this is not the wording you used, of course you'll have some difficulties in explaining what "stressed" would mean if it's not in your mind. We can check later on, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, whether, of course, "stressed" and "stretched" are quite similar to each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: I do understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may proceed in questioning, although "stressed" might not be the beginning of the answer of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Well, I'm not that stressed.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: In answer to your question, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, either stressed or stretched, I meant they were very thinly placed along the front line. Okay. One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, to make up for time, Mr. President, I'll put another question or put it differently. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Witness, do you know how many soldiers numbered the troops of Sarajevo at that time, how many men did the troops at Sarajevo at that time have? What were their numbers?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know. I was not involved in their statistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Witness, am I correct in recalling and in saying that you stated yourself that you had seen, on several occasions, tanks in action, and more specifically, close to the Jewish cemetery area?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion above the Jewish cemetery, yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: On one particular occasion you stated that you were able to observe these tanks well because you had, I think you said, telescopic sights with you, telescopic lenses. Is that true?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. I had a high-resolution Nikon lens on my Nikon camera.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you. So you had your photograph -- your camera with you?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Did you take photographs of the tank?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took photographs of the firing, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: My question did not have to do with the firing but the tank itself.

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't take any pictures of the tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: So you were in action, you saw the tank, you are a wartime photographer, and you did not take photographs of the tank. Is that how I am to understand what you said?

utterances.speaker: JOHN ASHTON [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not take pictures of that tank.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I should like to give the witness a number of other exhibits to look at. Do I have your authorisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would like to know in advance whether you are going to just have them marked for identification or you want to tender them into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Here is my answer. Previously, the exhibit that I read out from, we would like to tender it into evidence, and it is D12.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness statement that was -- yes?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that is correct. Mr. Roy Thomas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Thomas. Do you have it, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I just returned that one to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I remembered. So you want to tender that into evidence. We'll do that at the end of your cross-examination, but at least give a prenumbered copy, D12, to the Registry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can hand it over right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the other exhibits that I wish to present the witness with are photographs, for the most part, and as far as possible, I should like the witness to answer in technical terms and to give quite specific answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
